title: Anomalous Local Heat Capacity and Bipartite Entanglement
authors: Jake Xuereb, A. de Oliveira Junior
abstract: The heat capacity of a system quantifies how it energetically responds to changes in temperature at equilibrium. Whilst this quantity is positive and even additive for non-interacting systems, self-gravitating systems such as stars or subsystems of strongly interacting quantum systems are known to have negative or anomalous specific heat capacities. In this work, we investigate how the presence of entanglement at equilibrium can influence how an interacting system responds energetically to changes in temperature. We examine the local heat capacity of interacting quantum systems providing an analytical understanding for when anomalies occur. Most interestingly, we find a connection between local heat capacity anomalies and entanglement by deriving a separability bound based on the fluctuations of local and interaction energies. We illustrate our results with two examples (i) a nearest neighbour spin-1/2 chain and (ii) two coupled quantum harmonic oscillators. Lastly, we provide an information-theoretic formula connecting mutual information and athermality to the non-additivity of the heat capacity. Our results provide model-independent thermodynamic entanglement detection bounds and insight into the relationship between quantum correlations and the heat capacity of quantum systems.
summary: This work establishes a quantitative link between quantum entanglement and the local heat capacity of interacting quantum systems. By deriving a separability bound based on energy fluctuations, the authors show that anomalous local heat capacities can serve as a thermodynamic witness for quantum correlations. This offers a powerful, general tool for characterizing quantum states using measurable thermal properties.
main_problem: The paper investigates how quantum entanglement at equilibrium influences the local heat capacity of interacting quantum systems, particularly focusing on the occurrence of anomalous (negative) heat capacities.
main_result: A model-independent separability bound is derived connecting local heat capacity fluctuations to entanglement, showing that violations of this bound detect quantum correlations.
method: The authors use thermodynamic identities relating heat capacity to covariance and variance, deriving separability bounds based on local uncertainty relations for the system's energy operators.
model_or_system: The study analyzes bipartite interacting quantum systems, exemplified by nearest neighbour spin-1/2 chains, coupled quantum harmonic oscillators (QHOs), and general Hamiltonians $H = H_A + H_B + H_{	ext{int}}$.
key_observables: Local Heat Capacity ($C_X(T)$), Global Heat Capacity ($C(T)$), Mutual Information, and the separability bound derived from energy fluctuations.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$) or inverse temperature ($ eta$), interaction strength ($J, \chi$), and the nature of the coupling ($H_{	ext{int}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is primarily restricted to equilibrium states ($ho_ eta$) and bipartite systems, although the derived bounds are claimed to be model-independent.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that local heat capacities can be anomalous in interacting systems, and they compare entanglement detection using the derived heat capacity bound against other criteria like the PPT boundary.
paper_structure: The paper develops the general framework by defining local heat capacity and deriving its decomposition. It then establishes the separability bound using fluctuation relations, applying this bound to specific models like spin chains and QHOs to demonstrate the connection between entanglement and thermodynamic anomalies.
why_interesting: It provides a novel, model-independent thermodynamic diagnostic tool—the local heat capacity bound—to detect quantum entanglement, bridging concepts from quantum information theory and classical thermodynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Anomalous heat capacity meets entanglement. At thermal equilibrium, (i) the global heat capacity C(T) (orange curve) of a noninteracting bipartite system is the sum of its local heat capacities, whereas (ii) in the presence of interactions, C(T) need not to be equal to the sum of the local contributions. Although the global heat ca- pacity remains nonnegative, a local heat capacity can become anoma- lous, i.e., negative, as illustrated by CA(T) (purple curve). Here, we investigate when such anomalous local thermal responses are con- nected to entanglement.
